fact: The real test draws on the whole handbook, including the opening chapter on values, permanent residence and the test itself.
Applicants for permanent residence or citizenship must be able to speak and read English and know about everyday life in the UK.
As of January 2013 there were two ways to prove those skills: pass the Life in the UK test, or complete an ESOL with Citizenship course.
The test questions need English at ESOL Entry Level 3, so no separate English language test was needed (as of 2013).
Work-visa holders (for example on points-based Tier 1 and Tier 2) usually have to pass the test before they can settle permanently.
The ESOL with Citizenship course is for people whose English is below Entry Level 3, and it ends with a test.
After passing, you apply for permanent residence or citizenship; the form, evidence and fee depend on your circumstances and the type of application.
Forms and fees were listed on the UK Border Agency website; that agency no longer exists, so use current official guidance.
From October 2013, settlement needs the test plus proof of speaking and listening English at level B1 of the CEFR, equal to ESOL Entry Level 3.
The rules for citizenship may be updated later, so read current official guidance before you apply.
The test is made of 24 questions, taken from every part of the handbook, on key topics of British life.
The 24 questions differ from person to person at each test session.
English is the normal language of the test, though arrangements exist for taking it in Welsh or Scottish Gaelic.
Only approved, registered centres may run the test, and the UK has roughly 60 of them.
The test can only be booked online, and only certificates from registered test centres are accepted.
Residents of the Channel Islands or the Isle of Man have different arrangements for taking the test.
Bring ID and something that proves where you live; without them you cannot sit the test.
Each section ends with a 'Check that you understand' box; these are only prompts, and revising nothing but their points would leave you short of what the test covers.
The handbook's language is pitched at ESOL Entry Level 3, so anyone at that level or higher should be able to read it.
The test lasts 45 minutes (from official test information; this PDF does not state it).
The pass mark is 75%, which is 18 correct answers out of 24 (from official test information; this PDF does not state it).

Five principles underpin British life, as the handbook lists them: individual liberty, the rule of law, democracy, taking part in community life, and tolerance of people with other faiths and beliefs.
The values come from Britain's history and traditions, and law, custom and shared expectations protect them.
Extremism and intolerance are not accepted in British society.
New citizens promise at the ceremony to be loyal to the UK, respect its rights and freedoms, uphold democracy, obey the law and carry out their duties as citizens.
Residents are expected to obey the law, respect other people's rights (including their freedom to hold their own views) and treat people fairly.
Residents should also look after themselves and their family, and look after their local area and the environment.
The UK in turn guarantees freedom to hold any faith or belief, freedom of speech, and protection against unfair discrimination.
Further UK rights include a fair trial and a say in choosing the government through elections.
Chapter 1 covers the rights and responsibilities that apply to everyone living in the UK, whether citizen or not.
Applying to settle or become a citizen is a serious commitment to accept the duties of living here and to respect UK law, values and customs.
Shared values include obeying and respecting the law, respecting others' rights, treating others fairly, behaving responsibly, and helping and protecting your family.
More shared values: look after the environment, give everyone equal treatment whatever their class, disability, age, religion, race, sex or orientation, and earn a living for your family.
Shared British values also include helping other people and voting in local and national elections.
England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland together make up the UK.
The rest of the island of Ireland is an independent country and is not part of the UK.
Officially the country is the United Kingdom (UK) of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
'Great Britain' means England, Scotland and Wales only; it does not include Northern Ireland.
In the handbook the words 'Britain' and 'British' are used for everyone in the UK (the printed sentence is garbled in this PDF and mentions 'Isles').
The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands have close ties to the UK, but they are not part of it.
The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands govern themselves and are known as Crown dependencies.
Overseas territories around the world, for example St Helena and the Falkland Islands, have ties to the UK but do not form part of it.
Parliament, meeting at Westminster, governs the UK as a whole.
Each of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has a parliament or assembly with devolved powers over set areas.
Expect questions on how Great Britain, the British Isles and Britain differ, and on what the Crown dependencies are.
The first people in Britain were hunter-gatherers, in the period called the Stone Age.
For much of the Stone Age a land link joined Britain to mainland Europe, and people trailed herds of deer and horses.
Around 10,000 years ago the sea (the Channel) cut Britain off from mainland Europe for good.
Farming reached Britain roughly 6,000 years ago.
The early farmers' forebears probably originated in the south-east of Europe.
Early farming settlers built houses, burial tombs and large monuments.
On the Orkney islands north of Scotland, Skara Brae is northern Europe's finest surviving prehistoric village.
Digging at Skara Brae shows archaeologists daily life in the late Stone Age.
Stonehenge, a monument built by early farmers, still stands in Wiltshire, England.
Stonehenge may have been a place where people gathered for ceremonies at certain times of the year.
People learned to make bronze about 4,000 years ago, beginning the Bronze Age.
Bronze Age homes were roundhouses, and the dead were laid in mounds called round barrows.
Bronze Age metalworkers made tools, ornaments and weapons in bronze and gold.
The Iron Age followed the Bronze Age, when people learned to make weapons and tools from iron.
In the Iron Age people lived in roundhouses grouped into larger settlements, some defended as hill forts.
Maiden Castle in Dorset is an impressive Iron Age hill fort that can still be seen.
Iron Age society was mainly made up of farmers, craftspeople and fighters.
Iron Age people spoke languages of the Celtic family; related languages are still spoken in parts of Wales, Scotland and Ireland.
The earliest coins struck in Britain date from the Iron Age; several carry the names of kings.
The first coins and kings' names mark the beginnings of British history.
In 55 BC Julius Caesar led an unsuccessful Roman invasion of Britain.
For nearly 100 years after Caesar's attempt, Britain remained separate from the Roman Empire.
In AD 43 the emperor Claudius himself took an army to Britain in a fresh attempt at conquest.
Despite resistance from some British tribes, the Romans occupied almost all of Britain.
The Romans remained in Britain for about 400 years.
Boudicca ruled the Iceni tribe of today's eastern England and fought the Romans.
Boudicca has a statue on Westminster Bridge in London, close to the Houses of Parliament.
Roman rule left roads, public buildings, a legal system and new species of plants and animals.
The first Christian communities appeared in Britain in the 3rd and 4th centuries AD, under Roman rule.
The Romans never took control of some northern areas, in today's Scotland.
Hadrian had a wall built across northern England as a barrier against the Picts, forerunners of the Scots.
Forts were part of the wall; remains of two, Housesteads and Vindolanda, are still visible.
Hadrian's Wall is a popular walking area and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Picts, who inhabited the area of present-day Scotland, are counted among the ancestors of the Scots.
In AD 410 the Roman troops pulled out of Britain to protect other provinces, and they did not come back.
Once the Romans were gone, Britain was attacked by peoples from northern Europe - the Jutes, Angles and Saxons.
Today's English grew out of the languages of the Jutes, Angles and Saxons.
Around AD 600 a number of Anglo-Saxon kingdoms existed, chiefly in the area of modern England.
Sutton Hoo, in Suffolk, is where an Anglo-Saxon king was laid in a ship with his wealth and war gear under an earth mound.
Parts of western Britain, including much of Wales, and Scotland stayed free of Anglo-Saxon rule.
The Anglo-Saxons arrived as non-Christians, and missionaries came to preach Christianity.
Missionaries from Ireland spread Christianity in the north of Britain.
St Patrick, one of the Irish missionaries, became the patron saint of Ireland.
St Columba set up a monastery on Iona, a small island off the Scottish coast.
St Augustine headed a mission from Rome that brought Christianity to southern Britain.
The first Archbishop of Canterbury was St Augustine.
The Vikings came from Denmark and Norway.
The Vikings first visited Britain in AD 789, raiding coastal towns and taking goods and slaves.
Later the Vikings stopped just raiding and started settling, founding communities in eastern England and Scotland.
The Danelaw was the area in the east and north of England where many Viking invaders stayed.
Place names such as Grimsby and Scunthorpe in the Danelaw come from the Viking languages.
The Viking newcomers blended in with the local people, and a number became Christians.
Fear of Viking attacks pushed the northern peoples to join together under a single ruler, Kenneth MacAlpin.
The term 'Scotland' began to be used for the country united under Kenneth MacAlpin.
King Alfred the Great beat the Vikings and brought the English Anglo-Saxon kingdoms together.
Anglo-Saxon kings stayed on the English throne apart from a brief spell of Danish rule.
The first of the Danish kings of England was Cnut, also spelled Canute.
In 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the Saxon king Harold at the Battle of Hastings.
Harold was killed at Hastings and William became king of England, known as William the Conqueror.
The Bayeux Tapestry, a huge embroidery still on display in France, commemorates the Battle of Hastings.
Since the Norman Conquest, no foreign army has successfully invaded England.
The Norman Conquest brought big changes to how England was governed and how society was organised.
The new rulers spoke Norman French, which shaped the English language as it grew.
Normans took Wales at first; over time the Welsh regained land.
The Scots and Normans fought on the border; the Normans took some border land but did not invade Scotland.
William had people list every town and village, who lived and owned land there and what animals they had; this Domesday Book survives today.
The medieval period, from the Norman Conquest until about 1485, saw fighting nearly all the time.
Kings of England battled nobles in Wales, Scotland and Ireland over who controlled their territories.
King Edward I issued the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284, and Wales was annexed to the Crown of England.
Huge castles, including Conwy and Caernarfon (spelled Caernarvon in the handbook), were built to maintain English power in Wales.
Around 1450 the final Welsh uprisings were put down, and Wales received English law and the English language.
Robert the Bruce led the Scots to victory over the English at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314.
After Bannockburn Scotland remained unconquered by the English.
Ireland began the Middle Ages as an independent country; English troops first arrived to help the Irish king, then stayed and built settlements of their own.
The Pale, an area around Dublin, was under English rule by 1200, and some lords elsewhere in Ireland recognised the English king's authority.
In the Crusades, European Christians (including many knights) fought to take the Holy Land.
The Hundred Years War between England and France was really 116 years long.
Agincourt (1415): Henry V's much smaller English force beat the French.
The English left France in the 1450s.
Under Norman feudalism lords held land from the king and in exchange had to provide soldiers when he needed them.
Few peasants owned land; most were serfs, tied to a lord's estate: they farmed a small plot but had to work for him and could not leave.
A similar feudal system grew up in southern Scotland, whereas in northern Scotland and Ireland the land belonged to clan members (clans being leading families).
The Black Death, probably plague, arrived in Britain in 1348.
The Black Death killed about one third of the population of England, with a similar proportion in Scotland and Wales.
After the plague less grain was needed, workers were scarce and peasants asked for better pay.
New social classes appeared, including large landowners later called the gentry, and growing wealth in towns created a strong middle class.
The Black Death killed many people in the Pale, in Ireland, and for a while the area under English control got smaller.
Parliament grew out of the king's circle of advisers, which included barons and senior churchmen, during the Middle Ages.
There were few formal limits on the king's power until 1215.
King John's nobles compelled him in 1215 to accept a charter of rights, Magna Carta ('the Great Charter').
Magna Carta set the principle that the king himself had to obey the law.
Magna Carta safeguarded noblemen's rights and meant the king could not tax or make laws without involving them.
English kings called parliaments to consult their nobles, particularly when they needed to raise money.
Bishops, nobles and large landowners sat in the House of Lords.
Knights (mostly smaller landowners) and rich townspeople sat in the Commons; very few people could vote for them.
Scotland's Parliament had three Estates: lords, commons and clergy.
In the Middle Ages the idea took hold that judges should act independently of the government.
In England judges developed common law through precedent, meaning following earlier decisions, and tradition.
Scotland's legal system developed differently, with laws codified, meaning written down.
After the Conquest the king and nobles spoke Norman French and the peasants spoke Anglo-Saxon; the two gradually combined into English.
Park and beauty come from Norman French; apple, cow and summer come from Anglo-Saxon.
Modern English often has two similar words, one French and one Anglo-Saxon, such as 'demand' and 'ask'.
By about 1400 official papers in England were written in English, and the court and Parliament preferred it.
Geoffrey Chaucer wrote the Canterbury Tales in English before 1400: poems about pilgrims travelling to Canterbury who tell each other stories.
William Caxton, who introduced printing with a press to England, was among the first to print the Canterbury Tales.
In Scotland Gaelic continued and the Scots language developed; The Bruce, by John Barbour, tells of the Battle of Bannockburn.
Many castles went up across Britain and Ireland, partly for defence; most are ruins now, but Windsor and Edinburgh are still used.
Great medieval cathedrals such as Lincoln were built and are still used for worship; some had stained glass windows, as at York Minster.
In the Middle Ages England sold large amounts of wool abroad and was a major trading country.
Skilled newcomers included Italian glass makers, Dutch canal builders, French weavers and German engineers.
The Wars of the Roses was a civil war that began in 1455 over who should be king, fought between the Houses of Lancaster and York.
Lancaster's badge was a red rose; York's was a white one.
The Wars of the Roses ended at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485, where King Richard III of York was killed.
As King Henry VII, Henry Tudor (leader of the House of Lancaster) became the first Tudor king and founded the House of Tudor.
Henry VII married Richard III's niece, Elizabeth of York, uniting the two families.
The Tudor emblem put a white rose inside a red one, showing that York and Lancaster were now allies.
Henry VII built a stronger central government and weakened the nobles after winning the crown.
Henry VII was careful with money and built up the Crown's financial reserves.
Henry VIII went on centralising power; he is best known for splitting from the Church of Rome and for his six marriages.
Henry's first wife, Catherine of Aragon, was a Spanish princess; only their daughter Mary survived, so he divorced her hoping for a son.
Anne Boleyn, Henry's English second wife, bore Elizabeth; she was accused of having lovers and was executed at the Tower of London.
Henry's third wife, Jane Seymour, gave him his son Edward but died shortly after the birth.
Henry's fourth wife, Anne of Cleves, was a German princess; he married her for political reasons and divorced her soon after.
Catherine Howard, Anne Boleyn's cousin, became wife number five; like Anne, she faced accusations of lovers and was put to death.
Catherine Parr, Henry's last wife, was a widow; she outlived him, remarried and died shortly afterwards.
During Henry VIII's reign the Act for the Government of Wales formally united Wales with England; Wales sent members to the Commons and its legal system was reformed.
When the Pope refused to approve his divorce, Henry established the Church of England.
In the Church of England the king, not the Pope, appoints bishops and orders how people should worship.
The Reformation was a European movement against the Pope's authority and against Roman Catholic Church ideas and practices.
Protestants set up separate churches, read the Bible in their own language rather than Latin, rejected prayer to saints and shrines, and stressed a personal bond with God.
During the 1500s Protestantism spread steadily in England, Wales and Scotland.
Henry VIII was succeeded by his strongly Protestant son Edward VI, who died aged 15 after ruling just over six years.
The Book of Common Prayer was written for the Church of England under Edward VI, and some churches still use a version of it.
Edward's half-sister Mary, a devout Catholic, became queen and persecuted Protestants, earning the name 'Bloody Mary'.
Mary's half-sister Elizabeth, the child of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, followed her on the throne.
Protestant Elizabeth I restored the Church of England to official status; attendance at church was compulsory but she did not probe people's private beliefs.
Elizabeth balanced the views of Catholics and more extreme Protestants and so avoided serious religious conflict in England.
Elizabeth became one of England's most popular monarchs, particularly after the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588.
In 1588 England defeated the Spanish Armada, a big fleet Spain dispatched to conquer the country and bring back Catholicism.
Sir Francis Drake, one of the commanders who defeated the Armada, was a founder of England's naval tradition.
Drake's Golden Hind was among the first ships to circumnavigate (sail all the way round) the globe.
Under Elizabeth national pride grew; seafarers searched for fresh trading routes and tried to do business in Spain's American colonies.
English settlers began colonising America's east coast during Elizabeth's reign, and the movement grew much larger in the 1600s.
In 1560 the mainly Protestant Scottish Parliament abolished the Pope's authority in Scotland and made Catholic services illegal.
Scotland got an established Protestant Church; unlike England's, it was not a state Church (the handbook's wording on its leadership is garbled).
Mary Stuart, a Catholic, became Scotland's queen as a baby, aged just seven days, because her father died.
Mary spent much of her childhood in France; after her husband was murdered and she was suspected of involvement, she fled to England.
Mary gave up the throne in favour of her Protestant son, James VI of Scotland.
Elizabeth feared her cousin Mary wanted the English crown, held her captive for 20 years, and finally had her executed for plotting.
William Shakespeare (1564-1616) was born in Stratford-upon-Avon and was a playwright, actor and poet.
Among Shakespeare's best-known plays are Hamlet, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet and A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Shakespeare wrote about history but also showed everyday people, not only royalty, and was among the first to do so.
Many words in everyday English were coined by Shakespeare, who had a strong effect on the language.
'Once more unto the breach' is from Henry V, 'To be or not to be' from Hamlet, and 'A rose by any other name' from Romeo and Juliet.
'All the world's a stage' is from As You Like It, and 'The darling buds of May' is from Sonnet 18.
London's Globe Theatre is a modern reconstruction of the type of playhouse in which Shakespeare's plays were first staged.
Elizabeth I remained unmarried and childless; at her death in 1603 the throne passed to her cousin, King James VI of Scotland.
James VI of Scotland also became James I of England, Wales and Ireland, while Scotland stayed a separate country.
Elizabeth I managed Parliament skilfully, balancing her views against the Lords and the increasingly Protestant Commons.
In this period Ireland was almost completely Catholic, and Henry VII and Henry VIII extended English control over the whole country.
Henry VIII called himself King of Ireland; English law was brought in, and local chiefs had to take orders from the Lord Lieutenants in Dublin.
English attempts to impose Protestantism and English inheritance laws led Irish chieftains to rebel, followed by brutal fighting.
Protestants from Scotland and England were encouraged by the English government to settle in Ulster on land taken from Catholic landholders; these settlements were called plantations.
Many of the Ulster planters came from the south-west of Scotland; London companies were granted other land.
James I later organised similar plantations in other parts of Ireland, with serious long-term consequences.
James I and his son Charles I believed in the Divine Right of Kings: the idea that the king was appointed directly by God to rule.
James I and Charles I believed they could rule without asking Parliament to agree.
James I's reign produced a new English Bible translation, the King James Version or Authorised Version, still used in many Protestant churches.
Charles I inherited the crowns of England, Wales, Ireland and Scotland and attempted to govern by the Divine Right of kings.
Because Parliament disagreed with his religious and foreign policy, Charles I governed without calling it for 11 years, finding other ways to raise money.
Charles I wanted more ceremony in worship; his attempt to impose a revised Prayer Book on Scotland's Presbyterian Church caused serious unrest.
A Scottish army was formed, and in 1640 Charles recalled Parliament to ask it for money for his own army.
Many MPs were Puritans, Protestants who wanted strict and simple doctrine and worship, and they disliked the king's Church reforms.
Parliament still would not grant him funds, even when a Scottish army crossed into England.
A fresh revolt broke out in Ireland, where Catholics were afraid of the Puritans' growing power.
Seizing the moment, Parliament asked to take command of the English army, a step that would have shifted significant power from the king to itself.
Charles I went to the Commons to arrest five opposition MPs, but they had received a warning and were not present.
Since Charles I's failed arrest attempt, no king or queen has entered the House of Commons.
In 1642 the king and Parliament went to war with each other.
The king's supporters were called Cavaliers and Parliament's supporters were called Roundheads.
Defeats at Marston Moor and Naseby broke the king's army, and Parliament was clearly victorious by 1646.
Charles I refused any agreement with Parliament and was executed in 1649.
England became a republic, the Commonwealth, once the king was executed, and had no monarch.
Parliament sent General Oliver Cromwell to Ireland, where the 1641 revolt was still under way and a Royalist army remained.
Cromwell established Parliament's authority in Ireland with such violence that he is still a controversial figure there.
The Scots had not approved of the king's execution; they proclaimed Charles II and crowned him king of Scotland, and he marched a Scottish army into England.
Cromwell defeated Charles II's Scottish army at the Battles of Dunbar and Worcester.
Charles II fled after Worcester, at one point hiding in an oak tree, and eventually got away to the Continent.
As Lord Protector, Cromwell led the republic until he died in 1658.
Oliver's son Richard took over as Lord Protector but failed to keep the army and the government in line.
Britain was a republic for 11 years, the only period in its history without a monarch, and people began to talk about needing a king.
In May 1660 Parliament invited Charles II back from exile in the Netherlands, and he was crowned king of England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland.
Charles II told people he did not want to go into exile again, and understood he sometimes had to reach agreement with Parliament.
Following the Restoration the Church of England regained its place as the established Church, while Catholics and Puritans were excluded from power.
In 1665 a major outbreak of plague killed thousands of people in London, especially in poorer areas.
Fire swept through London in 1666, burning down much of the city, including St Paul's Cathedral and many churches.
Sir Christopher Wren, the architect, designed the new St Paul's Cathedral when London was rebuilt.
Samuel Pepys recorded the plague and the fire in a diary that was published later and is still read.
The Habeas Corpus Act (1679) made unlawful imprisonment illegal.
Habeas corpus is Latin for 'you must produce the person in court'; every prisoner is entitled to a hearing.
The Royal Society, founded under Charles II to advance 'natural knowledge', is the world's oldest scientific society still in existence.
Edmund Halley, an early Royal Society member, correctly forecast the comeback of what is now Halley's Comet.
Isaac Newton (1643-1727), born in Lincolnshire and educated at Cambridge, showed in his Principia how gravity applies to the whole universe.
Newton also found that white light is a mixture of rainbow colours.
Charles II died in 1685 without legitimate children and his Roman Catholic brother became King James II of England, Wales and Ireland and James VII of Scotland.
James II favoured Catholics, let them be army officers against an Act of Parliament, did not seek agreement with Parliament and arrested some bishops.
James's heirs were two Protestant daughters, but when his wife had a son it seemed the next monarch might be a Catholic.
James II's older daughter Mary had married her cousin William of Orange, who was the Protestant ruler of the Netherlands.
In 1688 leading English Protestants invited William to come over with an army and take the throne.
William met no opposition and James escaped to France; William and Mary ruled together, he as William III of England, Wales and Ireland and as William II of Scotland.
'Glorious' because England saw no fighting and Parliament's power was secured, so a monarch could no longer rule alone.
James II invaded Ireland with a French army but William defeated him at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690.
The Battle of the Boyne is still celebrated by some people in Northern Ireland today.
Following the Boyne, the Roman Catholic Church in Ireland faced many restrictions, and Irish Catholics were kept out of government.
The handbook says the Scots who rose for James in an armed rebellion were quickly beaten at Killiecrankie.
Scottish clans had to swear an oath accepting William as king; the MacDonalds of Glencoe were late and were all killed.
The memory of the Glencoe massacre made some Scots distrust the new government.
Supporters of James II were called Jacobites: a number followed him into exile in France, while others backed him secretly, especially in Scotland.
At William and Mary's coronation a Declaration of Rights said the king could no longer levy taxes or dispense justice without Parliament's consent.
The 1689 Bill of Rights set out Parliament's rights and put limits on the monarch.
Parliament now decided who could be king or queen, and the monarch had to be Protestant.
After 1689 elections had to be held at least every three years; the gap later became seven years and is now five.
The monarch had to seek Parliament's agreement each year to pay for the army and navy.
To rule effectively, a monarch relied on ministers who could win votes in both the Commons and the Lords.
The two main groups in Parliament were the Whigs and the Tories (the Conservative Party is still sometimes called the Tories), the beginning of party politics.
Newspapers could be published without a government licence after 1695, a step towards press freedom.
Legislation that followed the Glorious Revolution started the era of 'constitutional monarchy': the monarch remained influential but could not force through policies against Parliament's wishes.
After William III ministers slowly overtook the monarch in importance, although the country was still far from a modern democracy.
Few could vote: only men owning property above a set value; women had no vote.
A 'pocket borough' was an area under one rich family's control; a 'rotten borough' had almost no voters.
Jews were allowed to settle in London again in 1656, the first to do so in Britain since medieval times.
Between 1680 and 1720 many Huguenots, French Protestants persecuted for their religion, came to Britain; many were skilled scientists, bankers or weavers.
Many British and Irish people emigrated to colonies such as those in America, while other people moved into Britain.
Queen Anne, William and Mary's successor, had no surviving children, which created uncertainty over the succession.
The Act of Union, called the Treaty of Union in Scotland, was agreed in 1707 and created the Kingdom of Great Britain.
From 1707 Scotland lost its independence but retained separate law, schools and its Presbyterian Church.
Queen Anne died in 1714, and Parliament picked a German, George I, as king, as he was her nearest Protestant relative.
Scottish Jacobites tried to replace George I with James II's son but were swiftly beaten.
George I spoke poor English, so he depended even more on his ministers.
The leading minister came to be called the Prime Minister; Sir Robert Walpole, in office 1721 to 1742, was the first to hold that title.
Charles Edward Stuart (Bonnie Prince Charlie), a grandson of James II, landed in Scotland in 1745 aiming to replace George II with a Stuart king.
Charles was supported by Highland clansmen, raised an army and at first had some successes.
George II's army defeated Charles at the Battle of Culloden in 1746 and Charles escaped back to Europe.
After Culloden the clans lost power: chieftains who had the English king's favour became landlords and clansmen became tenants who paid for their land.
During the 'Highland Clearances' landlords tore down small farms (crofts) to make space for sheep and cattle; evictions were frequent in the early 1800s and many Scots emigrated to North America.
The Scottish poet Robert Burns (1759-96), called 'The Bard' in Scotland, wrote in Scots, in English with some Scottish words, and in standard English.
Burns rewrote many old folk songs, changing or adding words.
Robert Burns is best remembered for the song Auld Lang Syne, sung at New Year (Hogmanay in Scotland) in the UK and abroad.
New thinking about politics, philosophy and science in the 18th century is called the Enlightenment; many leading figures were Scots.
Adam Smith developed economic ideas that are still referred to today.
David Hume wrote about human nature, and philosophers are still influenced by his ideas.
James Watt's steam power work helped drive the Industrial Revolution.
An Enlightenment idea still important in the UK: people may hold their own political and religious views, and the state should not force beliefs on them.
Until the 1700s farming was Britain's biggest source of jobs, with cottage industries in which cloth and lace were made at home.
The Industrial Revolution (18th and 19th centuries) was a rapid growth of British industry.
Britain was the world's first large-scale industrial nation.
Machines and steam power made industrialisation possible.
New factories ran on coal and raw materials, drawing large numbers of people off the land to work in mining and manufacturing.
The Bessemer process for mass-producing steel led to the growth of shipbuilding and the railways.
Factory and other manufacturing work became Britain's main kind of employment.
Richard Arkwright (1732-92), a former barber and wig-maker, moved into textiles and improved the carding machine.
Arkwright developed horse-driven spinning mills and later used steam engines to power machinery.
Arkwright is best remembered for running efficient, profitable factories.
Canals linked factories with towns and ports, especially in the new industrial areas of the Midlands and north.
Working conditions in the Industrial Revolution were very poor: no laws protected employees, hours were long and work dangerous, and children worked like adults or worse.
Captain James Cook charted Australia's coast, and some colonies were founded there.
Britain won Canada, and the East India Company, begun as a trading firm, took control of much of India.
Colonies were also founded in southern Africa.
Britain imported sugar and tobacco from North America and the West Indies, and textiles, tea and spices from India and Indonesia.
Overseas trade and settlement sometimes set Britain against France, which was expanding in the same regions.
Sake Dean Mahomet (1759-1851), from Bengal, opened London's Hindoostane Coffee House in 1810, Britain's first curry house, and brought 'shampooing' (head massage) to Britain.
Slavery was banned inside Britain, yet by the 1700s Britain and the American colonies ran a huge overseas slave trade.
Slaves came mainly from West Africa on British ships and worked on tobacco and sugar plantations in America and the Caribbean.
Quakers formed the first organised anti-slavery societies in the late 1700s and petitioned Parliament for a ban.
William Wilberforce, an evangelical Christian and MP, helped change opinion and the law against the slave trade.
A law of 1807 made it illegal to carry slaves in British ships or trade them from British ports.
The Emancipation Act of 1833 ended slavery across the whole British Empire.
The Royal Navy intercepted other nations' slave ships, freed the captives and punished the slavers.
After 1833 some 2 million Indian and Chinese workers took the freed slaves' place on plantations, in mines and on railways.
By the 1760s the rich American colonies largely governed themselves and resisted British taxes: 'no taxation without representation'.
In 1776 thirteen American colonies declared independence, and Britain recognised it in 1783 after the colonists defeated the British army.
After the French Revolution of 1789 the new French government declared war on Britain, and Napoleon, who became Emperor, continued the war.
In 1805 Britain's navy beat combined French and Spanish fleets at the Battle of Trafalgar; Admiral Nelson commanded and was killed.
London's Trafalgar Square has Nelson's Column in his memory, and visitors can tour his ship HMS Victory at Portsmouth.
In 1815 the French Wars ended when the Duke of Wellington defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo; Wellington, the 'Iron Duke', later became Prime Minister.
Ireland had shared a monarch with England and Wales since Henry VIII, but in 1801, after the Act of Union of 1800, it joined Great Britain in the United Kingdom (UK) of Great Britain and Ireland.
The Union Flag, often called the Union Jack, combined the crosses associated with England, Scotland and Ireland and is still the UK's official flag.
St George, patron saint of England, is symbolised by a white flag bearing a red cross.
Scotland's patron saint, St Andrew, is shown as a white diagonal cross on blue.
Ireland's patron saint, St Patrick, is shown as a red diagonal cross on white.
The Welsh dragon is not on the Union Flag because Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was made in 1606.
Queen Victoria came to the throne at 18 in 1837 and ruled until 1901, almost 64 years, which in 2013 was longer than any other British monarch.
In the Victorian Age Britain increased in power abroad, the middle classes grew in importance, and reformers worked to improve life for the poor.
Under Victoria the Empire spread over all India, Australia and much of Africa, the biggest empire in history, home to an estimated 400 million-plus people.
From 1853 to 1913 up to 13 million Britons emigrated.
Roughly 120,000 Russian and Polish Jews fled persecution to Britain between 1870 and 1914, many to London's East End, Manchester and Leeds.
People from imperial lands such as India and Africa also moved to Britain to work, live and study.
Britain promoted free trade, for example by repealing the Corn Laws in 1846, which had blocked imports of cheap grain.
A law of 1847 capped women's and children's working hours at ten a day.
The railway engine was pioneered by father and son George and Robert Stephenson shortly before Victoria's accession; railways spread widely during her reign.
Isambard Kingdom Brunel (1806-59), a Portsmouth-born engineer, designed tunnels, bridges, railways and ships.
Brunel built the Great Western Railway, Britain's first major railway, which ran from Paddington Station in London to Wales, the West Midlands and the south-west of England.
In the 1800s Britain made over half of all the iron, coal and cotton cloth produced worldwide, and became a financial centre for banking and insurance.
The Great Exhibition opened in 1851 in Hyde Park, housed in the Crystal Palace, an enormous building of steel and glass; most exhibits were made in Britain.
Britain, Turkey and France fought Russia in the Crimean War (1853-1856), the first war to be covered widely by the media.
Illness spread in Crimean War hospitals killed more soldiers than wounds did.
Queen Victoria introduced the Victoria Cross during the Crimean War to honour acts of valour by soldiers.
Florence Nightingale (1820-1910), born in Italy to English parents, trained as a nurse in Germany and in 1854 worked in military hospitals in Turkey, reducing the death rate.
In 1860 Nightingale set up the first nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London, and she is regarded as modern nursing's founder.
In 19th-century Ireland two-thirds of people lived by farming, often on very small plots, and many depended heavily on potatoes.
Mid-century, Ireland's potato crop failed and famine followed: roughly one million died and a further 1.5 million emigrated.
Irish emigrants went to the United States and England; by 1861 there were large Irish populations in Liverpool, London, Manchester and Glasgow.
The Fenians wanted complete Irish independence, while Charles Stuart Parnell favoured 'Home Rule', with Ireland staying in the UK but having its own parliament.
The 1832 Reform Act widened the vote, ended pocket and rotten boroughs and shifted seats to towns and cities.
After 1832 voting was still based on owning property, so the working class still could not vote.
The Chartists campaigned for the vote for working-class men and others without property, presenting petitions to Parliament that at first seemed unsuccessful.
The Reform Act of 1867 created many more urban seats and cut the property needed to vote, but most men still could not vote and no women could.
Politicians realised they had to persuade more voters, so parties began creating organisations to reach ordinary voters; universal suffrage followed in the next century.
A wife's wages and property automatically passed to her husband until 1870.
Laws passed in 1870 and 1882 allowed married women to keep what they earned and owned.
Women's campaigning for the vote grew from the late 1800s into the early 1900s, and members of the suffrage movement were called suffragettes.
Some supporters said the Empire boosted trade and commerce, while others thought it over-expanded and a drain on resources, yet most British people saw it as a force for good.
The Boer War of 1899 to 1902 was fought in South Africa against settlers of Dutch origin called Boers; it lasted over three years and made the Empire's future more urgent.
Mostly peacefully, the Empire became a Commonwealth in the later 1900s as countries were given independence.
Rudyard Kipling (1865-1936), born in India, received the 1907 Nobel Prize in Literature; his writing reflected the idea that the Empire was a force for good.
Kipling's books include The Jungle Book and the Just So Stories; his poem 'If' regularly ranks as a national favourite.
The Empire went on expanding up to the 1920s.
Victorian times brought better housing for workers and improved transport for people and goods.
Many American colonists came from families who had gone to North America for religious freedom; they were educated people with a strong attachment to liberty.
Britain in the early 1900s felt confident: it had a huge Empire, a respected navy, booming industry and stable institutions, making it a 'superpower'.
Early 1900s reforms brought help for jobless people, state pensions for the old and free school meals.
Other early reforms improved workplace safety, tightened town planning to stop slums, and gave mothers and children better support after divorce or separation.
Local councils became more democratic, and MPs began to receive a salary, which opened public life to more people.
Emmeline Pankhurst (1858-1928) was born in Manchester; in 1889 she founded the Women's Franchise League to win local-election votes for married women.
In 1903 Emmeline Pankhurst co-founded the Women's Social and Political Union; its members were the first to be called suffragettes.
Suffragettes broke the law in protest: chaining themselves to railings, smashing windows and setting fires; many, Emmeline among them, refused food in prison.
Women over 30 won the vote and the right to become MPs in 1918, partly as thanks for their war work in the First World War.
Shortly before Emmeline Pankhurst's death in 1928, women gained the vote at 21, the same age as men.
On 28 June 1914 the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria set off the chain of events that led to the First World War (1914-18).
Further causes of the First World War: rising nationalism, militarism, imperial rivalry and two opposing alliances of great powers.

Britain was an Allied Power with France, Russia, Japan, Belgium and Serbia (later Greece, Italy, Romania and the US), against the Central Powers led by Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire.
The whole British Empire took part in the war; over a million Indian soldiers fought for Britain and about 40,000 died.
Men from Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Africa and the West Indies also fought alongside the British.
Britain suffered more than 2 million casualties in the First World War.
On the first day of the British attack at the Somme (July 1916) there were about 60,000 British casualties.
On 11 November 1918, at 11.00 am, the First World War ended with victory for Britain and its allies.
In 1913 Britain promised Ireland 'Home Rule': its own parliament, with Ireland remaining in the UK.
Protestants in the north of Ireland opposed the Home Rule Bill and threatened to resist it by force; the First World War led the government to postpone changes.
In 1916 Irish Nationalists, unwilling to wait, rose against the British in Dublin in the Easter Rising; its leaders were executed under military law.
After the Easter Rising, guerrilla fighting broke out between Irish forces and British troops and police in Ireland.
A treaty in 1921 brought peace, and by 1922 Ireland had split into two separate countries.
The six mainly Protestant counties in the north stayed in the UK as Northern Ireland.
The Irish Free State, with its own government, was formed from the rest of Ireland, and it became a republic in 1949.
Anger about the division led to a campaign of terror in Northern Ireland and beyond; the struggle between nationalists wanting Irish unity and loyalists to Britain is called 'the Troubles'.
Housing got better for many people in the 1920s, with more public housing and new houses in towns and cities.
The worldwide 'Great Depression' began in 1929 and caused mass unemployment in parts of the UK.
The 1930s depression hit heavy industries such as shipbuilding badly, while new industries, including cars and aviation, developed.
Falling prices left workers with more spare money; between 1930 and 1939 the number of cars went from 1 million to 2 million, and many houses were built.
Culture flourished between the wars; Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh were leading writers.
John Maynard Keynes, an economist, put forward economic theories that became influential in these years.
BBC radio began in 1922, and in 1936 the BBC launched the first regular TV service anywhere.
John Logie Baird (1888-1946), a Scot, developed TV in the 1920s; in 1932 he transmitted the first TV broadcast from London to Glasgow.
Scot Sir Robert Watson-Watt suggested radio waves could spot enemy planes, and radar was first tested successfully in 1935.
Alan Turing imagined the 'Turing machine' in the 1930s, a mathematical idea that fed into computer science and today's computers.
Sir Frank Whittle, an RAF engineer officer, developed the jet engine in Britain during the 1930s.
The Scottish physician and researcher John MacLeod co-discovered insulin, used to treat diabetes.
Ernest Rutherford's teams, at Manchester and later Cambridge, were first to 'split the atom' and contributed to the Manhattan Project (the US atom bomb programme).
Alexander Fleming (1881-1955), born in Scotland, discovered penicillin in 1928 while researching influenza.
Howard Florey and Ernst Chain turned penicillin into a practical medicine, made in bulk by the 1940s; Fleming took the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
In 1933 Adolf Hitler gained power in Germany; he thought the conditions after the First World War were unfair and wanted more land for Germans.
Britain sought to avoid war, but declared it together with France after Hitler invaded Poland in 1939.
In the Second World War the Axis powers were fascist Italy and Germany plus the Empire of Japan; the main Allies were the UK, France, Poland, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.
Hitler took over Austria and Czechoslovakia, attacked Poland, seized Belgium and the Netherlands, and in 1940 beat the Allied armies in France.
In the national crisis of 1940 Winston Churchill took over as Prime Minister and led Britain through the war.
A vast naval evacuation took British and French troops off Dunkirk; civilian volunteers in small boats helped save over 300,000.
Despite heavy losses of life and equipment, the evacuation worked, and it gave us the expression 'Dunkirk spirit'.
Britain and the Empire faced Nazi Germany almost alone between late June 1940 and Germany's attack on the Soviet Union in June 1941.
The RAF won the vital air 'Battle of Britain' in summer 1940; Germany had to gain command of the skies before it could attempt an invasion.
The Spitfire and the Hurricane, both designed and built in Britain, were the RAF's most important aircraft in the Battle of Britain.
After the Battle of Britain the German air force kept bombing London and other cities at night, which was called the Blitz.
Coventry was nearly wiped out in the Blitz; other cities, notably London's East End, also suffered heavy damage.
People still say 'Blitz spirit' when Britons unite to cope with hardship.
Winston Churchill (1874-1965) was a soldier and journalist before becoming a Conservative MP in 1900, and became Prime Minister in May 1940.
Churchill refused to surrender to the Nazis and inspired the British people; he lost the 1945 election but returned as Prime Minister in 1951.
A state funeral followed Churchill's death in 1965, and in 2002 the public voted him the greatest ever Briton.
Famous Churchill lines include 'blood, toil, tears and sweat' (first speech as PM), 'we shall fight on the beaches' (after Dunkirk) and 'so many owed so much to so few' (Battle of Britain).
Japan defeated Britain at Singapore, then occupied Burma and threatened India.
America joined the war in December 1941 after Japan attacked its Pearl Harbour naval base.
Hitler invaded the Soviet Union in 1941 in history's biggest invasion; German forces were driven back with enormous losses, a turning point of the war.
The Allies slowly gained the advantage, with major victories in North Africa and Italy.
Allied troops came ashore in Normandy on 6 June 1944, commonly known as 'D-Day'.
Germany was comprehensively defeated by the Allies in May 1945.
In August 1945 the war with Japan finished after American atomic bombs hit the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Voters chose a Labour government under Clement Attlee in 1945, which pledged to deliver the welfare state set out in the Beveridge Report.
Clement Attlee (1883-1967) was Churchill's wartime Deputy Prime Minister, became Prime Minister in 1945, held the post until 1951 and was Labour Party leader for 20 years.
Attlee was born in London, trained as a barrister, did social work in East London and became a Labour MP; his government also nationalised industries and improved workers' conditions.
The 1942 Beveridge Report (Social Insurance and Allied Services), ordered by the wartime government in 1941, provided the foundation for the welfare state.
The Beveridge Report said the government should fight five 'Giant Evils': Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness.
William Beveridge (1879-1963) was an economist and social reformer who sat as a Liberal MP and later led the Liberals in the House of Lords.
In 1948 Aneurin 'Nye' Bevan, the Health Minister, set up the NHS, which guarantees everyone a basic standard of care with no charge at the time of use.
A national benefits system, 'social security', was meant to protect people 'from the cradle to the grave'.
After 1945 the state took the railways, coal mines and the gas, water and electricity industries into public ownership (nationalisation).
The 1944 Education Act (the 'Butler Act') made secondary schooling free in England and Wales.
R A Butler (1902-82), a Conservative MP responsible for education from 1941, oversaw the Education Act; the primary and secondary school divide it created still remains in most areas.
Nine countries, among them India, Pakistan and Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), became independent in 1947; more colonies followed in the next two decades.
Britain built its own atomic bomb and also joined NATO, an alliance created in response to the feared danger of attack by the Soviet Union and its allies.
The Conservatives governed Britain from 1951 to 1964; the 1950s brought economic recovery and growing prosperity for working people.
Prime Minister Harold Macmillan gave a well-known 'wind of change' speech supporting independence for Empire countries.
Short of labour after the war, the government invited workers from Ireland and elsewhere in Europe to help with reconstruction.
West Indians were invited to take jobs in Britain from 1948.
In the 1950s industries advertised overseas: centres in the West Indies recruited bus drivers, and northern and Midlands firms sent agents to India and Pakistan for textile and engineering workers.
For about 25 years people came to work and settle in Britain from India, Pakistan, the West Indies and, later, Bangladesh.
New laws in the late 1960s curbed immigration; newcomers needed a close link to Britain by birth or descent, so numbers fell.
Even so, about 28,000 people of Indian origin expelled from Uganda were admitted to Britain in the early 1970s.
The 1960s were called 'the Swinging Sixties' because British fashion, film and pop music boomed.
Two well-known pop groups of the 1960s were The Beatles and The Rolling Stones.
People had more money in the 1960s and bought cars and household goods; modern building styles in concrete and steel, such as tower blocks, spread.
Laws on divorce and (in England, Wales and Scotland) abortion were relaxed in the 1960s.
Women gained at work in the 1960s as Parliament introduced equal pay and banned gender discrimination by employers.
The Welsh poet Dylan Thomas (1914-53) wrote the radio play Under Milk Wood and also Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night, a poem; he died aged 39 in New York and is remembered in Swansea.
Under Milk Wood was first performed after Thomas's death, in 1954; he wrote the poem for his dying father in 1952; Swansea has a statue and the Dylan Thomas Centre.
DNA's structure was worked out in 1953 by researchers in London and Cambridge; the Briton Francis Crick shared a Nobel Prize for it.
Sir Bernard Lovell's radio telescope at Jodrell Bank, Cheshire, was long the largest on Earth and still operates.
Sir Christopher Cockerell invented the hovercraft in the 1950s.
Britain and France built Concorde, the only supersonic airliner ever in passenger service: first flight 1969, passengers from 1976, withdrawn 2003.
The Harrier 'jump jet', which can take off straight up, was designed and developed in the UK.
James Goodfellow invented the cash-dispensing ATM, or 'cashpoint', in the 1960s; Barclays Bank in Enfield, north London, had the first one in use in 1967.
Patrick Steptoe and Robert Edwards led the way in IVF treatment; the first 'test-tube baby' arrived at Oldham, Lancashire, in 1978.
Sir Peter Mansfield, a British scientist, co-invented the MRI scanner, which gives exact, non-invasive images of the body's internal organs.
In 1996 Sir Ian Wilmut (spelled Wilmot in the handbook) and Keith Campbell led a team that was the first to clone a mammal, Dolly the sheep.
The World Wide Web was invented by the Briton Sir Tim Berners-Lee; information was first transferred over it on 25 December 1990.
The post-war boom had ended by the late 1970s: prices rose sharply, the pound's value was unstable, and imports exceeded exports in value (a 'balance of payments' problem).
Many industries were hit by strikes in the 1970s, and people began to argue that the trade unions were too powerful.
The Northern Ireland Parliament was suspended in 1972, and from then on the UK government ruled Northern Ireland directly.
About 3,000 deaths resulted from the violence in Northern Ireland over the decades following 1969.
Mary Peters (1939-), born in Manchester and raised in Northern Ireland, won Olympic gold in the pentathlon in 1972 and became a Dame in 2000.
In 1957 the European Economic Community was formed by France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
Britain stayed out of the EEC at first but joined it in 1973.
The handbook says the UK is a full EU member that does not use the euro; the UK has since left the EU (see Brexit entries).
Margaret Thatcher (1925-2013), daughter of a grocer from Grantham, Lincolnshire, qualified as both a chemist and a lawyer, entered Parliament in 1959 and led the Conservatives from 1975.
After the Conservative victory in 1979 Margaret Thatcher became the UK's first woman Prime Minister and the longest-serving Prime Minister of the 20th century, until 1990.
Thatcher worked closely with US President Reagan and was among the first Western leaders to welcome the Soviet leadership changes that ended the Cold War.
Thatcher's government privatised nationalised industries and legally limited trade union powers; deregulation made the City of London a major financial centre.
Under Thatcher, old industries like shipbuilding and coal mining shrank.
In 1982 Argentina seized the Falkland Islands (a British overseas territory located in the South Atlantic), and a UK naval task force won them back.
John Major followed Thatcher as Prime Minister and helped start the Northern Ireland peace process.
Roald Dahl (1916-90) was born in Wales to Norwegian parents, served in the RAF in the Second World War and wrote George's Marvellous Medicine and Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.
Tony Blair led the Labour Party to victory in 1997; Labour governed until 2010, with Gordon Brown taking over as Prime Minister in 2007.
Blair's government created a Scottish Parliament with significant lawmaking powers and a Welsh Assembly with fewer such powers but wide control of public services.
Building on the peace process, the Blair government helped secure the Good Friday Agreement, signed in 1998.
Elections for the Northern Ireland Assembly were held in 1999; it was suspended in 2002 and not reinstated until 2007.
Most Northern Ireland paramilitary groups have given up their weapons and no longer operate.
In 2007 Gordon Brown became the new Prime Minister.
In the 1990s Britain was a leading member of the coalitions that freed Kuwait after Iraq's 1990 invasion and that dealt with the former Yugoslavia.
From 2000 British forces joined the fight against terrorism in places such as Afghanistan and Iraq; combat troops pulled out of Iraq in 2009.
The UK took part in the International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan, a UN-mandated force of 50 nations; Afghans were due to take full security responsibility by the end of 2014.
In May 2010, for the first time since February 1974, no party won an overall majority; the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats formed a coalition and David Cameron became Prime Minister.

The Proms are a summer series of orchestral classical concerts lasting eight weeks, held at venues such as the Royal Albert Hall in London.
The Proms has been organised by the BBC since 1927.
The best-known concert of the series is the Last Night of the Proms; it and others are shown on television.
Henry Purcell (1659-95), Westminster Abbey's organist, composed church music and operas, creating a British style separate from continental Europe's.
George Frederick Handel (1695-1759) was born in Germany, lived in the UK for many years and took British citizenship in 1727.
Handel composed Water Music for King George I, and for George II he composed Music for the Royal Fireworks; both pieces remain very popular.
Choirs often perform Handel's oratorio Messiah, especially around Easter.
Gustav Holst (1874-1934) wrote The Planets, a suite themed on the planets, and adapted its Jupiter as the tune of the hymn 'I vow to thee my country'.
Sir Edward Elgar (1857-1934), born in Worcester, is best known for his Pomp and Circumstance Marches; the Last Night of the Proms usually features March No 1, 'Land of Hope and Glory'.
Ralph Vaughan Williams (1872-1958) composed for orchestra and choir, drawing strongly on English folk tradition.
Sir William Walton (1902-83) wrote everything from film scores to opera, including coronation marches for George VI and Elizabeth II, and works such as Façade and Balthazar's Feast.
Benjamin Britten (1913-76) is remembered chiefly for the operas Peter Grimes and Billy Budd.
Britten's A Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra is based on a piece by Purcell and introduces the sections of an orchestra.
Britten started the Aldeburgh Festival in Suffolk, now a music event of worldwide standing.
Folk, jazz and pop all thrived in Britain during the 20th century; British pop is heard worldwide, helped by the English language, cultural links and creativity.
From the 1960s British pop has been among the UK's major cultural exports, and groups like The Beatles and The Rolling Stones remain influential.
British pop kept innovating: examples are the boy and girl bands of the 1990s and the Punk movement of the late 1970s.
Big music venues are The O2 in Greenwich (south-east London), Wembley Stadium and, in Glasgow, the Scottish Exhibition and Conference Centre (SECC).
Music festivals fill the UK summer; they include the V Festival, Glastonbury and the Isle of Wight Festival.
Wales holds a yearly National Eisteddfod, a cultural festival of music, dance, art and performance mostly in Welsh, featuring major Welsh poetry competitions.
The Mercury Music Prize, presented every September, rewards the best album produced in the UK or Ireland.
Each year the Brit Awards recognise British music, with prizes such as best group and best solo artist.
There are theatres in most UK towns and cities, large and small, often showing both professional and amateur productions.
London's West End, also called 'Theatreland', is particularly well known for theatre.
Agatha Christie's whodunnit The Mousetrap opened in London's West End in 1952 and holds the record for the longest first run of any show.
Gilbert and Sullivan, working in the 19th century, composed comic operas that satirised current politics and culture, such as The Mikado, HMS Pinafore and The Pirates of Penzance.
Andrew Lloyd Webber wrote music for world-popular shows including Jesus Christ Superstar and Evita (with Tim Rice), Cats and The Phantom of the Opera.
Pantomime is a festive-season show drawn from fairy tales, mixing songs and jokes; classic roles are the Dame (a man dressed as a woman) and a two-person horse or cow costume.
The Edinburgh Festival is a series of arts and cultural festivals held in Edinburgh, Scotland, every summer.
The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is the largest and most famous of the Edinburgh festivals, featuring chiefly theatre and comedy, much of it experimental.
The Laurence Olivier Awards, held annually in London, have categories such as best director, actor and actress and are named after the actor Sir Laurence Olivier, known for Shakespeare roles.
Most medieval art was religious, notably church wall paintings and manuscript illustrations; much of it was lost after the Protestant Reformation.
During the 1500s and 1600s a lot of the painters active in Britain came from other countries, e.g. Hans Holbein and Sir Anthony Van Dyck.
From the 18th century British artists, particularly portrait and landscape painters, became well known.
Well-known galleries include the National Museum in Cardiff, Tate Modern, Tate Britain and the National Gallery in London, and Edinburgh's National Gallery of Scotland.
Set up in 1984 and named for Joseph Turner, the Turner Prize rewards contemporary art; four shortlisted works go on show at Tate Britain, and then the winner is revealed.
Winners of the Turner Prize have included Damien Hirst and Richard Wright; it ranks among Europe's most prestigious prizes for the visual arts.
Thomas Gainsborough (1727-88), a portraitist, frequently painted his sitters against a rural or garden backdrop.
David Allan (1744-96), a Scottish painter best known for portraits, painted The Origin of Painting.
Landscape artist Joseph Turner (1775-1851) was influential for his modern approach and helped raise the standing of landscape painting.
Landscape artist John Constable (1776-1837) is best remembered for his views of Dedham Vale, on the border between Suffolk and Essex.
In the later 1800s the Pre-Raphaelites painted richly detailed, vivid scenes from religion or literature; they included Holman Hunt, Dante Gabriel Rossetti and John Millais.
Sir John Lavery (1856-1941) was a successful Northern Irish portrait painter whose subjects included the Royal Family.
The English sculptor Henry Moore (1898-1986) is best known for his large abstract bronze sculptures.
The Welsh artist John Petts (1914-91) is remembered above all for engraving and stained-glass work.
German-born British artist Lucian Freud (1922-2011) is chiefly remembered for portraits.
David Hockney (born 1937) was an important contributor to the 1960s 'pop art' movement and is still influential.
Great medieval cathedrals that still stand include those at Durham, Lincoln, Canterbury and Salisbury.
William the Conqueror ordered the building of the White Tower, the Norman keep at the heart of the Tower of London.
Wealthier landowners put up grand country houses, Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire being one example.
Inspired by classical architecture, Inigo Jones designed the Banqueting House in Whitehall and the Queen's House at Greenwich in the 17th century.
Sir Christopher Wren developed a British form of the elaborate European style, as seen in the rebuilt St Paul's Cathedral.
Tastes shifted to plainer designs in the 1700s; Scottish architect Robert Adam styled interiors as well as exteriors, for instance at Dumfries House.
Robert Adam's approach shaped architects in places like Bath, home to the Royal Crescent.
The medieval 'gothic' style came back in the 1800s, used for the Houses of Parliament, St Pancras Station and town halls in Manchester and Sheffield.
In the 20th century Sir Edwin Lutyens designed New Delhi as the seat of government in India and, after the First World War, many war memorials including the Cenotaph in Whitehall.
Each year the monarch, politicians and foreign diplomats gather at the Cenotaph for the Remembrance Day service.
Modern British architects such as Dame Zaha Hadid, Lord (Richard) Rogers and Sir Norman Foster work on major projects worldwide.
In the 1700s Lancelot 'Capability' Brown shaped country-house grounds to appear natural (lawns, trees, lakes); his nickname came from saying sites had 'capabilities'.
Gertrude Jekyll created colourful gardens to go with houses by the architect Edwin Lutyens, with whom she frequently collaborated.
Garden designers from Britain and abroad display their work each year at the Chelsea Flower Show.
Thomas Chippendale designed 18th-century furniture, and Clarice Cliff designed Art Deco ceramics.
Sir Terence Conran was a 20th-century interior designer.
Vivienne Westwood, Alexander McQueen and Mary Quant are leading recent fashion designers.
Sir William Golding (novelist), Seamus Heaney (poet) and Harold Pinter (playwright) are British winners of the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Agatha Christie's detective novels have readers worldwide, while Ian Fleming created the character James Bond.
A 2003 national vote named JRR Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings the UK's favourite novel.
Since 1968 the Man Booker Prize for Fiction has gone to the best novel by an author from Ireland, Zimbabwe or the Commonwealth; winners include Julian Barnes, Hilary Mantel and Ian McEwan.
Jane Austen (1775-1817), an English novelist, wrote Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility, which are about marriage and family relationships.
Charles Dickens (1812-70) wrote Oliver Twist and Great Expectations; his characters Scrooge (a mean person) and Mr Micawber (always hopeful) feature in everyday talk.
Robert Louis Stevenson (1850-94) wrote Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Kidnapped and Treasure Island.
Thomas Hardy (1840-1928), author and poet, wrote novels about rural society, such as Jude the Obscure and Far from the Madding Crowd.
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (1859-1930), a Scottish doctor and author, invented Sherlock Holmes, among the earliest detectives in fiction.
Evelyn Waugh (1903-66) wrote satires including Decline and Fall and Scoop, though Brideshead Revisited is probably his best-known work.
Sir Kingsley Amis (1922-95), an English novelist and poet, is best known for his novel Lucky Jim.
Graham Greene (1904-91) drew on his faith in his novels, which include Our Man in Havana, The Honorary Consul, The Heart of the Matter and Brighton Rock.
J K Rowling (born 1965) wrote the Harry Potter children's books, which have been a huge international success.
Beowulf, an Anglo-Saxon poem about a hero fighting monsters, continues to be translated into present-day English.
Surviving medieval poems include Chaucer's Canterbury Tales and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, about a knight at King Arthur's court.
Besides his plays, Shakespeare composed numerous sonnets - poems with exactly 14 lines.
John Milton, inspired by his religious views as Protestant ideas spread, wrote Paradise Lost.
William Wordsworth found inspiration in nature; Sir Walter Scott wrote verse about Scotland and the Scotland-England borderlands, and mostly set his novels in Scotland.
Popular 19th-century poets included Robert and Elizabeth Browning, Alfred Lord Tennyson, Percy Shelley, Lord Byron, John Keats and William Blake.
Wilfred Owen and Siegfried Sassoon are two of the poets who wrote about what they lived through in the First World War.
Ted Hughes, Sir John Betjeman, John Masefield and Walter de la Mare are more recent popular poets.
Poets' Corner, in Westminster Abbey, holds the graves or memorials of many famous poets.

Christmas Day is a public holiday on 25 December, when Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus Christ.
Christmas traditions: a big meal (often roast turkey with Christmas pudding and mince pies), presents and cards, decorated homes and trees, and Father Christmas delivering gifts to children.
A lot of Christians attend church on Christmas Eve (24 December) or Christmas Day.
Boxing Day (26 December) is the public holiday that follows Christmas Day.
Easter (March or April) commemorates Jesus Christ's death on Good Friday and his resurrection on Easter Sunday.
Good Friday and Easter Monday are public holidays.
Lent is the 40 days before Easter, a time to reflect and prepare; traditionally people fasted and today many give up something such as a favourite food.
Shrove Tuesday (Pancake Day) falls on the eve of Lent; pancakes were made to finish off eggs, fat and milk before the fast began.
Ash Wednesday starts Lent; Christians are marked on the forehead with an ash cross, symbolising death and regret for sin.
Chocolate Easter eggs are given as gifts as a sign of new life, and non-religious people enjoy them too.
Hindus and Sikhs celebrate Diwali, the Festival of Lights, for five days in October or November, marking good triumphing over evil and the acquiring of knowledge.
Leicester holds a famous Diwali celebration.
Hannukah (Hanukkah) falls in November or December, lasts eight days and recalls the Jewish struggle for religious freedom; a candle is lit daily on an eight-branched stand (menorah).
Eid al-Fitr celebrates the close of Ramadan, a month of fasting for Muslims, who give thanks to Allah for the strength to finish it; the date moves each year.
Eid ul-Adha recalls the prophet Ibrahim's readiness to give up his son at God's command; many Muslims slaughter an animal for food, which in Britain has to take place in a slaughterhouse.
Vaisakhi (or Baisakhi) is a 14 April Sikh festival marking the founding of the Khalsa community, with parades, dancing and singing.
1 January, New Year's Day, is a public holiday, and most celebrations happen the night before, on New Year's Eve (31 December).
Scots call 31 December Hogmanay and also get 2 January as a public holiday; to some of them it is a bigger occasion than Christmas.
Valentine's Day (14 February) is when couples swap cards and presents, and admirers may post an unsigned card to a person they secretly like.
On 1 April, April Fool's Day, pranks are played until noon, and TV and newspapers often carry spoof stories.
Mothering Sunday (Mother's Day) falls on the Sunday three weeks ahead of Easter; children give their mothers cards or gifts.
Father's Day takes place on the third Sunday of June, with children giving their fathers cards or presents.
Halloween, 31 October, is an ancient festival with roots in a pagan festival marking the start of winter; young people dress up for 'trick or treat' and many carve pumpkin lanterns.

Bonfire Night, 5 November, is marked in Great Britain with fireworks; it recalls the failed Gunpowder Plot of 1605, when Catholics led by Guy Fawkes tried to blow up the Protestant king in Parliament.
On 11 November, Remembrance Day, the UK honours people killed in war on behalf of Britain and its allies; the day began with the First World War dead.
Bank holidays are non-religious public holidays on which banks and many businesses shut; they come in early May, late May or early June, and August.
Northern Ireland also has a public holiday in July that marks the Battle of the Boyne's anniversary.
On Remembrance Day people wear red poppies, observe a two-minute silence at 11.00 am and lay wreaths at the Cenotaph in Whitehall, London.
Some people rent extra land called an allotment to grow fruit and vegetables.
Famous gardens to visit include Mount Stewart in Northern Ireland, Bodnant Garden in Wales, Crathes Castle and Inveraray Castle in Scotland, and in England Kew Gardens, Sissinghurst and Hidcote.
Each UK country has a flower, sometimes worn on saints' days; the PDF's table is missing (official text: England rose, Scotland thistle, Wales daffodil and leek, Northern Ireland shamrock).
Most towns have a central shopping area called the town centre, most shops open seven days a week with reduced Sunday and public-holiday hours, and many towns have street markets.
England is traditionally linked with roast beef, potatoes, vegetables and Yorkshire puddings; fish and chips is another favourite.
Welsh cakes, a traditional snack of flour, dried fruit and spices served hot or cold, are associated with Wales.
Haggis, a Scottish dish, is a sheep's stomach filled with offal, suet, onion and oatmeal.
Northern Ireland is associated with the Ulster fry, a fry-up of bacon, eggs, sausage, black and white pudding, tomatoes, mushrooms, and soda and potato breads.
Buying alcohol in a pub or club requires you to be at least 18, though some pubs let under-18s in when accompanied by an adult.
From the age of 16, people may have beer or wine alongside a meal in a restaurant, a hotel, or the dining part of a pub, if an over-18 is with them.
Opening time for pubs is usually 11.00 am, or noon on Sundays; night clubs open and close later, and the licensee sets the exact hours.
Pubs are central to British social life and often the heart of a community; quiz nights are common, and darts and pool are the classic pub games.
Entry to a betting shop or gambling club is restricted to over-18s; many places also have casinos.
The National Lottery holds draws every week and can be entered with a ticket or scratch card; the minimum age rose from 16 to 18 in April 2021.
Treating a pet cruelly, or failing to look after it properly, is illegal.
A dog out in public needs a collar carrying its owner's name and address; owners must also control the dog and pick up its mess.
Vets (veterinary surgeons) provide vaccinations and treatment for animals, and certain charities assist owners who cannot pay for a vet.
The first public film screenings in the UK took place in 1896, and cinema soon caught on.
British film makers have been famous for clever special effects since the beginning, and this remains a British strength.
Sir Charles (Charlie) Chaplin found fame in silent films playing a tramp, one of numerous British actors who built careers in Hollywood.
British film studios thrived in the 1930s, with directors like Sir Alexander Korda and Sir Alfred Hitchcock; Hitchcock later moved to Hollywood and kept working until his death in 1980.
During the Second World War British films such as In Which We Serve helped boost morale.
Sir David Lean and Ridley Scott are later British directors who succeeded both at home and abroad.
British film comedy reached a high point in the 1950s and 1960s, with films such as The Ladykillers, Passport to Pimlico and the Carry On series.
Foreign companies often make films in the UK using British skills; the two top-earning film series, Harry Potter and James Bond, were produced here.
Ealing Studios can claim to be the world's longest continuously operating film studio.
Nick Park has won four Oscars for animated films, three of them for films featuring Wallace and Gromit.
Richard Burton, Sir Rex Harrison, David Niven and Sir Laurence Olivier were stars of many different kinds of popular film.
Tilda Swinton, Kate Winslet, Dame Judi Dench, Sir Anthony Hopkins and Colin Firth are recent British Oscar winners.
The British Academy Film Awards, hosted by BAFTA, are Britain's version of the Oscars.
The 39 Steps (1935) was directed by Alfred Hitchcock.
Brief Encounter (1945) was directed by David Lean.
The Third Man (1949) was directed by Carol Reed.
The Belles of St Trinian's (1954) was directed by Frank Launder.
Lawrence of Arabia (1962) was directed by David Lean.
Women in Love (1969) was directed by Ken Russell.
Don't Look Now (1973) was directed by Nicolas Roeg.
