Four Weddings and a Funeral (1994) was directed by Mike Newell.
Touching the Void (2003) was directed by Kevin MacDonald.
Humour has a long history: medieval kings and nobles kept jesters, Shakespeare wrote comic characters, and 1700s political cartoons mocked politicians and even the monarch.
The satirical magazine Punch was first published in the 1840s, and Private Eye continues the tradition of satire today.
Music hall was a popular type of variety show in Britain until television overtook it; Morecambe and Wise are among the performers who moved on to TV stardom.
Television comedy includes sitcoms about family life and the workplace, and satire shows such as That Was The Week That Was (1960s) and Spitting Image (1980s and 1990s).
In 1969 Monty Python's Flying Circus brought a new, progressive style of comedy, and stand-up has regained popularity lately.
Popular television programmes include the soap operas Coronation Street and EastEnders; some TV channels are free and others need a paid subscription.
Scotland has some Scotland-specific programmes and a Gaelic-language channel, Wales has a Welsh-language channel, and Northern Ireland has local programmes, some in Irish Gaelic.
A TV licence is required by anyone who watches TV on any device (TV, computer, etc.); it covers a single home, though separate tenants in a shared house need their own.
People over 75 could get their TV licence free and blind people paid half price; watching TV without a licence risks a fine of up to 1,000 pounds.
TV licence money pays for the BBC, a public service broadcaster of television and radio; BBC radio is also funded by licences.
The BBC is the world's largest broadcaster and the sole media organisation funded wholly by the state yet independent of the government; other channels rely on advertising and subscriptions.
There are many national and local radio stations; some specialise in particular music genres, some broadcast in Welsh or Gaelic, and stations other than the BBC's are funded by advertising.
Facebook and Twitter (now X) are popular social networks for keeping in contact, arranging events and sharing pictures, video clips and views.
Public footpaths criss-cross the UK, and there is scope for hill walking, mountain biking and mountaineering.
England, Wales and Scotland have 15 national parks, protected stretches of countryside open to all visitors, where people also live and work and help care for the landscape.
The National Trust for Scotland and the National Trust (which covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland) are two charities that protect significant buildings, stretches of coast and countryside.
Three volunteers set up the National Trust in 1895; today it depends on over 61,000 volunteers.
The name Big Ben properly belongs to the great bell in the Houses of Parliament's clock tower, though many people use it for the clock too.
More than 150 years old, the Parliament clock tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 to mark Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.
The Eden Project in Cornwall holds plants from around the globe in huge greenhouse-style biomes, and as a charity it runs environmental and social projects.
Edinburgh Castle towers over the city skyline, goes back to the early Middle Ages, and is managed by Historic Scotland, an agency of the Scottish government.
The Giant's Causeway on Northern Ireland's north-east coast is a set of columns formed from volcanic lava some 50 million years ago, and legends surround it.
Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park in western Scotland spans 720 sq miles (1,865 sq km); Loch Lomond is the biggest body of fresh water on mainland Britain.
The London Eye, a Ferris wheel 443 feet (135 metres) tall on the south bank of the Thames, was built for the millennium celebrations and is part of New Year celebrations.
Snowdonia National Park in North Wales covers 838 sq miles (2,170 sq km); Snowdon, Wales's highest peak, is its best-known landmark.
William the Conqueror began the Tower of London after taking the throne in 1066; today Yeoman Warders (Beefeaters) guide visitors, who can view the Crown Jewels.
At 885 sq miles (2,292 sq km), the Lake District is England's biggest national park, noted for its lakes and mountains; Windermere is its largest body of water.
Wastwater in the Lake District was chosen as Britain's favourite view by TV viewers in 2007.
Christianity is the UK's historic religion, and in the 2009 Citizenship Survey 70% of respondents described themselves as Christian.
The 2009 Citizenship Survey found Muslims 4%, Hindus 2%, Sikhs 1%, Jewish or Buddhist each under 0.5%, and 2% following another religion.
In the 2009 Citizenship Survey 21% of people said they had no religion.
Places of worship include mosques (Islam), synagogues (Judaism), Hindu and Buddhist temples and Sikh gurdwaras; the law gives everyone the right to follow a religion of their choice or none.
In England the Church and the state are constitutionally linked, and the official state Church is the Church of England (known as Anglican elsewhere and Episcopal in Scotland and the US).
Dating from the Reformation of the 1530s, the Church of England is a Protestant Church.
The Church of England has the monarch as its head, and the Archbishop of Canterbury is its spiritual leader.
Formally it is the monarch who selects the Archbishop and further top church officers, but in practice the Prime Minister and a committee set up by the Church make the choice.
Several bishops of the Church of England have seats in the House of Lords.
The Church of Scotland, a Presbyterian Church governed by ministers and elders, is Scotland's national Church.
The Church of Scotland's General Assembly is chaired by the Moderator, who serves a single year and often acts as the Church's spokesperson.
Neither Wales nor Northern Ireland has an established Church.
Other Protestant groups in the UK include Baptists, Methodists, Presbyterians and Quakers, and the biggest other Christian denomination is Roman Catholic.
St David's Day, 1 March, is the patron saint's day of Wales.
St Patrick's Day, 17 March, is the patron saint's day of Northern Ireland.
St George's Day, 23 April, is the patron saint's day of England.
St Andrew's Day, 30 November, is the patron saint's day of Scotland.
Only Scotland and Northern Ireland make the day of their patron saint (St Andrew, St Patrick) an official holiday; in Scotland some businesses stay open.

topic: Saints' days in England and Wales
fact: In England and Wales a patron saint's day is no longer a public holiday, although parades and small festivals still mark it.
Many major sporting events take place at stadiums such as the Millennium Stadium in Cardiff and Wembley Stadium in London.
A number of well-known sports originated in Britain: rugby, golf, football, cricket and lawn tennis among them.
The UK has hosted the Olympic Games three times: 1908, 1948 and 2012.
Britain finished third in the medal table at the 2012 Games, whose main Olympic site was in Stratford, East London.
The 2012 Paralympic Games were also held in London.
The Paralympics began at Stoke Mandeville hospital in Buckinghamshire, where Dr Sir Ludwig Guttman, a German refugee, encouraged spinal-injury patients to take part in sport.
In 1954 Sir Roger Bannister became the first person ever to run a mile in less than four minutes.
Scottish ex-racing driver Sir Jackie Stewart took the Formula 1 world title three times.
Bobby Moore was the captain of England's 1966 World Cup-winning football team.
Sir Ian Botham led England's cricket side as captain and set several English Test records, with both bat and ball.
Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean won Olympic gold for ice dancing in 1984 and four consecutive world championships.
Sir Steve Redgrave won gold medals in rowing at five consecutive Olympic Games.
Wheelchair athlete Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson collected 16 Paralympic medals (11 of them gold), six London Marathon victories and 30 world records.
Dame Kelly Holmes won two Olympic gold medals for running in 2004.
In 2004 Dame Ellen MacArthur set the record as the quickest solo sailor to circle the globe.
Sir Chris Hoy, a Scottish cyclist, won six Olympic gold medals and one silver and 11 world championship titles.
Wheelchair racer David Weir has six Paralympic golds, from two Games, and six London Marathon wins.
In 2012 Bradley Wiggins was the first British winner of the Tour de France; he has seven Olympic medals, including golds from 2004, 2008 and 2012.
Somalia-born British distance runner Mo Farah took the 5,000 m and 10,000 m titles at the 2012 Olympics, making him the first Briton to win Olympic 10,000 m gold.
Jessica Ennis won the 2012 Olympic heptathlon, an event with seven track and field disciplines.
Scottish tennis player Andy Murray won the 2012 US Open - Britain's first male Grand Slam singles champion since 1936 - and Olympic gold in the same year.
Ellie Simmonds took swimming golds at the 2008 and 2012 Paralympics; in 2008 she was the youngest on the British team.
Cricket began in England and is played in numerous countries today; a match may run for as long as five days and yet finish as a draw.
The Ashes is the most famous cricket competition, a series of Test matches between England and Australia.
'It's just not cricket', 'bowled a googly', 'playing a straight bat', 'batting on a sticky wicket' and 'rain stopped play' are all everyday phrases borrowed from cricket.
Football is the most popular sport in the UK, and the earliest professional clubs date from the late 1800s.
Each UK nation runs its own football leagues; the English Premier League draws an enormous worldwide audience, and British clubs also take part in the UEFA Champions League.
Each UK country has its own national football team, competing in tournaments such as the FIFA World Cup and the UEFA European Championships.
England's one and only major international tournament victory came at the 1966 World Cup, staged in the UK.
Rugby began in England in the early 1800s and comes in two forms with different rules: union and league.
Rugby has separate leagues and national teams for England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, though Northern Ireland plays with the Irish Republic.
Rugby union's best-known contest is the Six Nations Championship, in which England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy compete.
The Super League is the best-known rugby league club competition.
Horse racing has been run in Britain since Roman times and has strong, long-standing royal connections.
Royal Ascot, held over five days in Berkshire, is a race meeting that Royal Family members attend.
Aintree, near Liverpool, hosts the Grand National, while the Scottish Grand National is run at Ayr.
The National Horseracing Museum is in Newmarket, Suffolk.
Golf as we know it began in Scotland in the 1400s.
The Scottish town of St Andrews is called the home of golf.
The Open Championship is the only golf 'Major' held outside the United States, and a different golf course hosts it every year.
Today's tennis took shape in England during the late 19th century, and Leamington Spa saw the founding of the first tennis club in 1872.
Wimbledon is the world's oldest tennis tournament and the only Grand Slam event played on grass; the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club's grounds host it.
In 1966-67 Sir Francis Chichester became the first person to sail solo around the globe.
Two years after Chichester's voyage, Sir Robin Knox-Johnston was the first to complete a non-stop solo voyage around the globe.
The most famous British sailing event is held at Cowes on the Isle of Wight.
A popular yearly rowing race on the Thames is held between Oxford and Cambridge Universities.
British motor racing began in 1902, and the UK leads the world in designing and building motor-sport technology.
The UK stages a Formula 1 Grand Prix annually; British F1 World Champions have included Damon Hill, Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button.
Skiing is growing in popularity in the UK, with five ski centres in Scotland and, near Edinburgh, the longest artificial (dry) ski slope in Europe.
Because of immigration since the war, almost 10% of people in the UK have a parent or grandparent who was born overseas.
The UK is in north-western Europe; measured over the mainland, the longest distance is John O'Groats in Scotland to Land's End in England, about 870 miles (1,400 km).
The majority of Britons live in urban areas, yet a large part of the country remains rural, and many people go there to walk, camp and fish.

UK money is the pound sterling (written with the pound sign), divided into 100 pence.
UK coins are 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, one pound and two pounds.
UK banknotes are 5, 10, 20 and 50 pounds.
Scotland and Northern Ireland issue banknotes of their own that are valid throughout the UK, though shops and other businesses need not accept them.
People speak English with a wide range of accents and dialects in different parts of the UK.
Plenty of people in Wales speak Welsh, a language quite unlike English, and it is taught in both schools and universities.
Scottish Gaelic, yet another distinct language, is used in parts of the Highlands and Islands.
Irish Gaelic is spoken by some people in Northern Ireland.
The UK population in 1600 was just over 4 million.
The UK population in 1700 was 5 million.
The UK population in 1801 was 8 million.
The UK population in 1851 was 20 million.
The UK population in 1901 was 40 million.
The UK population in 1951 was 50 million.
The UK population in 1998 was 57 million.
The UK population in 2005 was just under 60 million.
The UK population in 2010 was just over 62 million.
The UK population in 2022 was estimated at 67.6 million.
The UK population has grown more quickly lately, driven by inward migration and people living longer.
England makes up about 84% of the UK population.
Roughly 5% of UK residents live in Wales, a little over 8% in Scotland and under 3% in Northern Ireland.
People are living longer than ever thanks to better living standards and health care, with a record number aged 85 and over, which affects pension and health costs.
The UK is ethnically diverse and changing quickly, especially in big cities like London; most people describe themselves as white, with large Asian, black and mixed groups.
By law, men and women must not be treated unfairly because of sex or marital status, and both have the same rights to work, hold property, marry and divorce.
Married parents share equal responsibility for their children.
Around half of UK workers are women, and on average girls finish school with stronger qualifications than boys.
Female students outnumber male ones at university, women are employed in every sector and hold more senior posts than before; men, too, now do a wider range of jobs.
People no longer assume a woman will stay at home; many continue working once they have children, and in lots of families both partners share childcare and housework.
The UK's system is a parliamentary democracy in which the monarch is head of state.
In a democracy every adult has a say, whether by voting directly on matters or by electing people to decide on their behalf.
Around 1800 only a small group had the vote: men aged over 21 holding property above a set value.
The franchise (everyone entitled to vote) widened in the 19th century, and parties began enrolling ordinary people of both sexes as members.
The Chartists campaigned for reform in the 1830s and 1840s; at that time their movement was widely regarded as having failed.
Chartist demands included votes for all men, annual elections, and equal treatment of all regions in the electoral system.
The Chartists also asked for voting in secret, the right for any man to stand for Parliament, and wages for MPs.
By 1918 most of the Chartists' reforms had been adopted.
The vote was extended to women over 30 in 1918.
From 1928 every man and woman aged over 21 could vote.
The voting age fell to 18 for both sexes in 1969.
A constitution lays down the principles a country is run by: its institutions, the limits on their power, and its laws and conventions.
No one document contains the British constitution, which is why it is called 'unwritten'.
The UK's constitution is unwritten largely because, unlike America or France, no revolution here created a wholly new system for good; institutions grew gradually over centuries.
Some people want a single written document, while others say an unwritten constitution allows more flexibility and better government.
The main parts of UK government are the monarchy, Parliament (Commons and Lords), the Prime Minister and cabinet, the judiciary, the police, the civil service and local government.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland also have devolved governments with the power to make laws on certain issues.
The UK's head of state, the monarch, also holds that role in a number of Commonwealth countries.
In a constitutional monarchy the king or queen reigns without ruling, and appoints whichever government the people elect in a democratic vote.
The monarch asks the person who leads the party holding the most MPs, or a coalition of parties, to become Prime Minister.
The monarch and Prime Minister meet on a regular basis; the monarch can give advice, warnings and encouragement, but policy is decided by the Prime Minister and cabinet.
Queen Elizabeth II reigned from her father's death in 1952, celebrated her Diamond Jubilee (60 years) in 2012, and died on 8 September 2022.
King Charles III has been sovereign since 2022; William, Prince of Wales, his elder son, is the heir, followed by William's children George, Charlotte and Louis.
The handbook text says that on his 59th birthday in 2023 Prince Edward became Duke of Edinburgh (the wording is garbled and should be checked).
As a ceremonial duty the monarch opens each new session of Parliament with a speech outlining what the government plans for the coming year.
Every Act of Parliament is passed in the monarch's name.
The monarch represents the UK to the world: receiving ambassadors and high commissioners, entertaining visiting heads of state and making state visits overseas.
While governments come and go, the monarch gives the country stability and continuity and acts as a rallying point for national identity and pride.
The UK's national anthem is 'God Save the King' ('Queen' when a queen reigns), played at major national occasions and when the monarch or Royal Family is present.
New citizens may swear by Almighty God to be faithful and bear true allegiance to the King, his heirs and successors, according to law.
Those who prefer not to swear a religious oath can instead solemnly affirm the same allegiance to the King, his heirs and successors.
For elections the UK is split into parliamentary constituencies, each choosing one Member of Parliament (MP) at a General Election; together the MPs make up the House of Commons.
Whichever party wins more than half the seats forms the government; with no outright majority, two parties may team up in a coalition.
The Commons is the more important chamber, since its members are elected by the people.
The Prime Minister and almost all members of the cabinet are MPs in the House of Commons.
Each MP represents a constituency; MPs represent everyone in it, help create new laws, scrutinise the government and debate important national issues.
Peers, as members of the House of Lords are known, are unelected and have no constituency.
Before 1958 every peer was a hereditary peer (title passed down), a senior judge or a Church of England bishop.
Life peers, appointed since 1958 by the monarch on the PM's advice, sit for their lifetime only; most have had major careers in politics, business, law or other professions.
The leaders of the remaining main parties can nominate some life peers, and an independent Appointments Commission nominates non-party ones.
In 1999 hereditary peers lost their automatic seats in the House of Lords; a small number, chosen by election among themselves, remain.
The Lords tends to be less tied to the government than the Commons is; it may propose amendments or new laws, which MPs then debate.
The Lords checks laws passed by the Commons to make sure they are fit for purpose and holds the government to account.
The House of Commons has the power to overrule the House of Lords, but rarely uses it.
The Speaker chairs the debates of the House of Commons and is the House's chief officer.
The Speaker stays politically neutral and speaks for no party, yet remains an MP with a constituency.
MPs choose the Speaker by secret ballot.
The Speaker keeps order in debates, makes sure the opposition has guaranteed time to debate issues it chooses, and represents Parliament on ceremonial occasions.
MPs are chosen in a General Election, which must take place at least once every five years.
If an MP dies or resigns, a by-election is held in his or her constituency.
The 'first past the post' system elects MPs: whoever gets the largest number of votes in a constituency wins that seat.
Usually the party that takes the most constituencies forms the government; when none wins a majority, two parties can combine as a coalition.
European Parliament elections were held every five years, electing Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) by proportional representation; the UK no longer takes part.
With proportional representation, each party's share of the seats matches its share of the total vote.
All elected members must serve their constituents; you can find contact details at your library or www.parliament.uk, and contact MPs at their constituency office or the House of Commons.
MPs, Assembly members, MSPs and MEPs often run 'surgeries' in their area, regular sessions where constituents can meet them face to face.
The Bill of Rights of 1689, the Habeas Corpus Act and Magna Carta are the roots of British rights and freedoms.
British diplomats and lawyers helped write the European Convention on Human Rights, which the UK signed in 1950 among the very first countries.
The European Convention on Human Rights guarantees, among other things, the right to life, a ban on torture, and a ban on slavery and forced labour.
The European Convention also protects liberty and security, a fair trial, freedom of expression, and the freedoms of thought, conscience and religion.
The Human Rights Act 1998 made the European Convention on Human Rights part of UK law; its principles bind the government, courts and other public bodies.
UK law bans unfair treatment, at work or in everyday life, based on race, sex, age, disability, religion or belief, sexuality, pregnancy and maternity, or marital status.
For discrimination problems contact the Citizens Advice Bureau or a body such as the Equality and Human Rights Commission (England, Wales, Scotland) or the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland.
Domestic violence is a serious crime: men or women who attack a husband, wife or live-in partner can be prosecuted.
A man who forces sex on a woman can be charged with rape, even if he is her husband.
Anyone facing domestic violence should get help quickly: a solicitor, the Citizens Advice Bureau, a refuge, the police, or the National Domestic Violence Freephone Helpline (24 hours, 0808 2000 247).
FGM (female genital mutilation) is against UK law, and both carrying it out and arranging for a girl or woman to be taken overseas for it are criminal offences.
Both partners must freely and fully consent to marry; arranged marriages are fine in the UK as long as both people agree.
A forced marriage is one where at least one person does not, or cannot, consent; making someone marry against their will is a crime.
In 2008, under the 2007 Act, Forced Marriage Protection Orders began in England, Wales and Northern Ireland; in Scotland they began in November 2011.
Breaking a Forced Marriage Protection Order is contempt of court and can mean up to two years in prison.
Income tax in the UK applies to wages, profits from self-employment, taxable benefits, pensions, and earnings from property, savings and dividends.
Income tax revenue funds public services like roads, education, the police and the armed forces.
HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) is the government department that collects taxes.
Most employees pay income tax through 'Pay As You Earn' (PAYE), where their employer takes the tax from their pay and sends it to HMRC.
People who work for themselves handle their own tax via 'self-assessment', filling in a tax return.
Almost everyone in paid work, including the self-employed, must pay National Insurance Contributions, which pay for benefits and services such as the state pension and the NHS.
Employers deduct employees' National Insurance Contributions from their pay, while the self-employed must pay their own.
Paying too little National Insurance can rule out contributory benefits, for instance Jobseeker's Allowance or a full state pension.
Your National Insurance number is a one-off personal account number so that your tax and contributions are recorded under your name; young people are sent one shortly before turning 16.
A non-UK national looking for or starting work, or self-employment, needs a National Insurance number, applied for through the DWP, but may start work without one.

topic: NI number is not a work permit
fact: Having a National Insurance number alone does not show an employer that you may legally work in the UK.
Driving a car or motorcycle needs a minimum age of 17, and a licence is required on public roads; mopeds can be ridden from 16.
Getting a UK driving licence means applying for a provisional licence first and then passing a theory test (multiple choice plus hazard perception) and a practical test.
A UK licence lasts until the holder is 70; after that it must be renewed every three years.
New drivers in Northern Ireland must show an 'R' (restricted driver) plate for twelve months after passing their test.
Licences issued in the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein or Norway stay valid in the UK until they expire; one from elsewhere works for 12 months, after which a UK licence is needed.
A UK-resident's car or motorcycle must be registered with the DVLA and have annual road tax paid (the handbook mentions a windscreen tax disc, which has since been abolished).
You must have valid motor insurance, and driving without insurance is a serious criminal offence.
Vehicles over three years old need a yearly Ministry of Transport (MOT) test, and lacking an MOT certificate is an offence.
Every UK resident has a core duty to understand and follow the law, and people who disregard it should not expect to gain permanent residence.
The law treats everyone in the UK equally, whatever their identity or origin.
Criminal law covers crimes; the police or another body, such as a council, normally investigate them and the courts impose punishment.
Civil law handles disagreements between individuals or groups.
Carrying any weapon is a crime, even in self-defence; this covers guns, knives and anything designed or modified to cause harm.
Buying or selling drugs like cannabis, cocaine, ecstasy and heroin is against UK law.
It is a crime to harass, alarm or distress someone because of their faith or ethnic background.
Tobacco may not legally be sold to under-18s.
Smoking tobacco is banned inside almost all enclosed public spaces in the UK.
Selling alcohol to anyone under 18, or buying it for them, is a crime, with one exception: from the age of 16 a person may have alcohol alongside a meal at a hotel or restaurant.
In certain areas, alcohol-free zones ban public drinking; police may take away alcohol or order young people to leave, and offenders can be fined or arrested.
Examples of civil law are housing disputes between landlords and tenants, consumer rights over faulty goods, employment disputes and debt.
Police duties are to safeguard people and property, keep the peace by preventing disorder, and prevent and detect crime.
The police are organised into separate forces headed by Chief Constables and are independent of the government.
In November 2012 the public in England and Wales elected Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs).
Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) determine local policing priorities and the budget, and choose the Chief Constable.
Police officers must obey the law, must not misuse their authority, lie, be rude or abusive or discriminate racially, and corrupt officers are severely punished.
Police community support officers (the handbook writes 'PSCOs') walk the beat, engage with the public, and help police officers when they attend crime scenes and large events.
After an arrest, at the police station an officer explains why you were arrested, and you may seek legal advice.
Complaints about the police can be made at a police station or in writing to the Chief Constable of the force involved.
Al Qa'ida, its affiliates and similar groups pose the gravest terrorist danger to the UK, though terrorism linked to Northern Ireland also exists.
Extremism is speaking or acting against core British values; examples include far-right and religious extremism.
Anyone who tries to recruit you to an extremist or terrorist cause should be reported to your local police.
Independent bodies for police complaints are the Independent Police Complaints Commission (England and Wales), the NI Police Ombudsman and the Police Complaints Commissioner for Scotland.
Judges, together called the judiciary, interpret the law and make sure trials are fair, and the government cannot interfere with this.
If judges agree a government action is illegal, it must change policy or ask Parliament to change the law; judges can also order public bodies to change practices or pay compensation.
Minor criminal cases are heard in a Magistrates' Court in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and in a Justice of the Peace Court in Scotland.
Magistrates and Justices of the Peace are local people, usually unpaid and without legal qualifications, who are trained and advised by a legal adviser; they decide verdict and sentence.
Minor cases in Northern Ireland go before a District Judge or Deputy District Judge, a paid, legally qualified professional.
Serious offences in England, Wales and Northern Ireland are tried at a Crown Court with a judge and jury.
Serious Scottish cases are heard at a Sheriff Court by a sheriff, sometimes with a jury, while the gravest, murder for example, go to the High Court before a judge and jury.
Juries are ordinary members of the public picked randomly from the local electoral register: 12 jurors in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, 15 in Scotland.
Anyone called for jury service has to serve unless ineligible (for instance, with a criminal conviction) or excused for a good reason such as poor health.
Juries weigh the evidence and return 'guilty' or 'not guilty' (Scotland also allows 'not proven'); after a guilty verdict the judge chooses the punishment.
In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, accused people aged 10 to 17 are normally heard in a Youth Court before up to three trained magistrates or a District Judge.
Parents or carers are expected to attend a Youth Court, the public cannot attend, and the young person's name and photograph cannot be published.
Scotland uses the Children's Hearings System for young offenders, and Northern Ireland uses youth conferencing.
County Courts deal with civil disputes such as recovering money owed, personal injury, family matters, breach of contract and divorce; in Scotland most of these go to the Sheriff Court.

topic: High Court and Court of Session
fact: More serious civil cases, such as claims for large compensation, go to the High Court in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and to the Court of Session in Edinburgh in Scotland.
Small claims is a relaxed way to resolve minor disputes without a lawyer: for claims below 10,000 pounds in England and Wales, and below 5,000 pounds in Scotland and Northern Ireland.
At a small claims hearing both parties sit around a table with the judge in a normal room, and a claim can be started online via Money Claims Online.
Solicitors are qualified lawyers who advise, act for clients and represent them in court; at the outset check what legal fields they specialise in and what it will probably cost.
The Citizens Advice Bureau or the Law Society (of England and Wales, of Scotland, or of Northern Ireland) can help you find a solicitor, whose charges are usually based on time spent.
The most serious cases involving young people aged 10 to 17 go to the Crown Court.
The Prime Minister (PM) heads the party in power, selects the cabinet and decides many significant public appointments.
10 Downing Street, close to the Houses of Parliament in central London, is the PM's official residence; Chequers is a country house outside London that the PM can also use.
A Prime Minister can be replaced when MPs of the governing party choose, or when he or she resigns, as usually happens after the party loses a General Election.
About 20 senior MPs are picked by the Prime Minister to run government departments as ministers, and these make up the cabinet.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy.
The Home Secretary's brief covers crime, policing and immigration.
The Foreign Secretary handles Britain's dealings with other countries.
Further ministers titled Secretaries of State run areas like education, health and defence.
The cabinet, a committee normally meeting each week, takes key decisions on government policy, many of which then need debate or approval in Parliament.
Each department also has Parliamentary Under-Secretaries of State and Ministers of State, who lead on specific parts of its work.
The opposition is the House of Commons' second-biggest party; its leader would normally become Prime Minister should the party win the next General Election.
Opposition MPs challenge the government's shortcomings at Prime Minister's Questions, a weekly session whenever Parliament sits.
The leader of the opposition appoints senior opposition MPs as 'shadow ministers', who form the shadow cabinet and challenge the government with alternative policies.
Anyone aged 18 or over may stand as an MP, but winning is unlikely without a major party's nomination.
The Conservative Party, the Labour Party and the Liberal Democrats are the main parties, alongside parties speaking for Scottish, Welsh or Northern Irish interests.
A small number of MPs sit outside the main parties as 'independents', usually standing for a cause that matters in their constituency.
The main parties seek members to take part in debates, contribute funds and help in election campaigns; most constituencies have a local branch, and each party holds a yearly policy conference.
Pressure and lobby groups try to influence government policy; examples are the CBI (for British business), Greenpeace (environment) and Liberty (human rights).
Civil servants help the government devise and implement policy and provide public services, answering to ministers.
Civil servants are appointed on merit and stay politically neutral, guided by four values: honesty, integrity, objectivity and impartiality.
Towns, cities and rural areas are run by elected councils called local authorities; some areas have district and county councils, while most large towns have one authority.
Local authorities supply a variety of services in their area, paid for by central government money plus local taxes.
A lot of councils name a mayor as ceremonial head, while in certain towns the mayor is an elected person who actually leads the administration.
London has 33 local authorities; policies across the capital are coordinated by the Mayor of London and the Greater London Authority.
Councillors are elected in May each year in most local authorities, and many candidates represent a political party.
From 1997 central government handed certain powers down (devolution), letting Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland decide more of the matters that directly concern them.
Wales has had an Assembly and Scotland a Parliament since 1999, and Northern Ireland has an Assembly that has sometimes been suspended.
The UK government keeps control of taxation, social security, defence, immigration and foreign affairs.
The devolved administrations, each with its own civil service, run many other public services, education among them.
Both the Welsh government and the National Assembly for Wales sit in Cardiff, Wales's capital.
The National Assembly for Wales had 60 members (AMs), chosen every four years under a proportional voting system.
Members of the Assembly may use Welsh or English, and everything the Assembly publishes appears in both.
In 20 subject areas, for example health and social services, education and training, housing and economic development, the Assembly can legislate for Wales.
From 2011 the National Assembly for Wales could make laws in its subject areas without needing the UK Parliament's consent.
The Scottish Parliament was formed in 1999 and sits in Edinburgh, the capital of Scotland.
There are 129 members (MSPs) in the Scottish Parliament, chosen under a proportional voting system.
Scotland's Parliament may legislate on anything not expressly reserved to Westminster - health, education, planning, and civil and criminal law - and has extra tax-raising powers.
Northern Ireland got its own Parliament in 1922 when Ireland was partitioned; it was scrapped in 1972, not long after the Troubles began in 1969.
The Northern Ireland Assembly came into being shortly after the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement of 1998, with power sharing that spreads ministerial posts across the main parties.
The Northern Ireland Assembly consists of 90 MLAs (Members of the Legislative Assembly), chosen through a proportional voting system.
Education, agriculture, the environment, and health and social services are among the matters the Northern Ireland Assembly decides.
The UK government is able to suspend any devolved assembly and has done so repeatedly in Northern Ireland; the handbook says the Assembly has worked successfully since 2007.
Parliament's debates are televised and written up in the official record known as Hansard.
Britain's press is free, so the government does not control what papers print; even so, some owners and editors campaign to sway government policy and public opinion.
The law requires radio and TV reporting on political parties to be balanced, with rival views given equal airtime.
The UK's voting rights became fully democratic in 1928, and the current voting age of 18 dates from 1969.
Adults who are UK citizens, or Commonwealth or Irish Republic citizens living in the UK, may vote in every public election.
Adult citizens of other EU states living in the UK could vote in all elections except General Elections.
You need to be on the electoral register to vote in parliamentary, local or European elections; sign up through your local council's electoral registration office.
Each September or October the electoral register is refreshed, with a form posted to every household.
Northern Ireland uses 'individual registration', where everyone entitled to vote completes their own form and stays registered while their details do not change.
Each local authority must let anyone view its electoral register under supervision, for example at council offices or some libraries.
People vote at polling stations (polling places in Scotland), where you receive a poll card beforehand and the station is open from 7.00 am to 10.00 pm on election day.
In Northern Ireland you must show photographic identification at the polling station.
Your ballot paper is marked in private in a polling booth; the decision is yours alone and nobody can insist you back a specific candidate.
If getting to a polling station is difficult you can register for a postal ballot.
Citizens of the UK, Irish Republic or Commonwealth who are 18 or older can mostly run for public office, apart from armed forces members, civil servants and those convicted of certain offences.
Lords members cannot run for the House of Commons, though every other public office is open to them.
Members of the public may sit in the public galleries of the Commons and Lords at the Palace of Westminster to hear debates, free of charge.
In Northern Ireland elected members, MLAs, meet in the Northern Ireland Assembly at Stormont in Belfast.
In Scotland the elected members, MSPs, meet in the Scottish Parliament building at Holyrood in Edinburgh.
In Wales the elected members, AMs, meet in the Welsh Assembly in the Senedd in Cardiff Bay.
Queues for the House of Commons can mean waiting one to two hours, while the House of Lords is usually easier to get into.
Commonwealth countries form an association that helps its members work toward democracy and development; most once belonged to the British Empire, though a few did not.
King Charles III, as monarch, is the Commonwealth's ceremonial head.
The handbook's text says the Commonwealth has 54 member states, but its own member table lists 56 (Gabon and Togo are in the table); check the current number.
Countries join the Commonwealth voluntarily; it cannot control them, but it is able to suspend a member.
The Commonwealth rests on core values: the rule of law, democracy and good government.
The Commonwealth member table groups members by region: Africa (21), Asia (8), Caribbean and Americas (13), Europe (3: Cyprus, Malta and the UK) and Pacific (11).
On 25 March 1957 the Treaty of Rome founded the European Economic Community (EEC), later the EU; its six signatories were France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
The UK joined the EU's predecessor body in 1973; after the Brexit referendum it left the EU officially on 31 January 2020 at 23:00 GMT.
According to the handbook, the EU now has 27 member states (alphabetically Austria to Sweden), with Croatia the most recent addition.
According to the handbook, UK law has included no general principles of EU law since 2024; the EU's own laws take the form of directives, regulations or framework decisions.
The Council of Europe, a body distinct from the EU with 47 member states (the UK among them), upholds human rights; it cannot make laws but drafted the European Convention on Human Rights.
The UN, founded after the Second World War to stop conflict and promote peace and security, is a global body with over 190 member countries.
The UN Security Council has 15 members and recommends action in international crises; the UK is one of its five permanent members.
NATO links European and North American states that promise mutual help if one is attacked and seek to keep the peace among themselves; the UK belongs.
Being a good neighbour means introducing yourself, respecting privacy, limiting noise, keeping your garden tidy, and putting rubbish out only when it is due to be collected.
Volunteering and helping your community helps you integrate and meet people, and fulfils the duties of being responsible and helping others.
People on the electoral register aged 18 to 70 can be randomly selected for jury service.
Parents can help in schools by assisting in classrooms, listening to children read, joining fundraising events or taking part in parent-teacher associations (PTAs).
School governors (school board members in Scotland) are community members who must be 18 or over when elected or appointed, with no upper age limit.
School governors do three main things: set the school's long-term direction, hold it to account, and monitor and assess how well it performs.
In England a free school can be set up on the application of parents or community groups, and anyone can apply online to be a governor.
Joining a political party shows support for its views and involves you in democracy; members may canvass, persuading voters by leaflet or door-knocking, and you need not say how you will vote.
British citizens can stand as a local councillor, an MP (or devolved equivalent) or an MEP; Irish and eligible Commonwealth citizens may also stand, and other EU citizens may except as an MP.
You can volunteer with local services such as hospitals and youth projects; universities, museums, housing associations and arts councils may seek volunteers for their boards.
Volunteering with the police is possible as a special constable or as a lay (non-police) representative, and you can also apply to be a magistrate.
Donated blood helps hospitals treat many injuries and illnesses; giving blood takes about an hour, and England and North Wales, rest of Wales, Scotland and NI each have a blood service.
Signing up on the organ donor register eases the decision for your family, and a living person may also give a kidney.
Volunteering offers friendships, English practice, job skills and a stronger CV, and improves your community.
Volunteer activities include working with animals, youth work, litter pick-ups, helping the homeless, mentoring (for example ex-prisoners), working in hospitals and helping older people.
British charities include the British Red Cross, Age UK (older people), the NSPCC (children) and Crisis and Shelter (the homeless).
Other charities include Friends of the Earth (environment), the National Trust, Cancer Research UK (medical research) and the People's Dispensary for Sick Animals (PDSA).
The National Citizen Service is for teenagers aged 16 and 17, combining outdoor activities, new skills and a community project.
Recycling saves energy, avoids extracting more raw materials and reduces rubbish going to landfill.
Shopping locally supports local businesses and farmers and cuts your carbon footprint, and walking or using public transport creates less pollution than driving.
